topic_tag: a minor character's function in a novel
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
blank_sentence: In an often-cited essay, one critic calls the gardener the novel's ______.

worlds.passage: A nineteenth-century novel follows two sisters who inherit a country estate, and the family's gardener speaks fewer lines than any other recurring character. The novel is told entirely through his letters to a brother overseas, so readers meet the sisters only as he describes them. Critics have noted that the elder sister, whom the letters treat warmly, comes across as generous, while the younger, whom he distrusts, seems grasping in scenes where the two behave almost identically. In an often-cited essay, one critic calls the gardener the novel's ______.
worlds.explanation: Every scene reaches the reader through the gardener's letters, and his feelings color how each sister appears even when they act alike, so he is the novel's "prism." "Pivot" fails because no single act of his turns the plot. "Pawn" fails because no one is described as using him for their ends. "Puzzle" fails because his attitudes are plain; it is the sisters who are seen through them.

pivot.why: his role runs through the whole book as its medium, not as one turning point

pawn.quote: readers meet the sisters only as he describes them
pawn.why: he shapes how others are seen rather than being moved about by them

puzzle.why: his likes and distrusts are stated openly, so his attitudes are not a mystery

worlds.passage: A nineteenth-century novel follows two sisters who inherit a country estate, and the family's gardener speaks fewer lines than any other recurring character. He appears in only one chapter, the eleventh of twenty-two, when he walks into the magistrate's office to say that he witnessed the old master sign a later will. In the ten chapters before it, the sisters' fortunes rise as their claim to the estate gains support; in the eleven after it, a cousin's lawsuit built on that later will strips them of nearly everything. In an often-cited essay, one critic calls the gardener the novel's ______.
worlds.explanation: The gardener's single appearance sits at the exact middle of the book, and the sisters' fortunes rise before it and collapse after it, so he is the novel's "pivot." "Prism" fails because he appears in one chapter and the story is not seen through him. "Pawn" fails because he comes forward on his own with what he saw. "Puzzle" fails because nothing about his act is left unexplained.

prism.quote: He appears in only one chapter
prism.why: a character present in one chapter cannot be the lens through which the whole story is viewed

pawn.quote: walks into the magistrate's office to say
pawn.why: he comes forward himself with what he witnessed; no one is shown moving him

puzzle.quote: a cousin's lawsuit built on that later will
puzzle.why: the consequences of his testimony are laid out plainly, with no unexplained mystery about him

worlds.passage: A nineteenth-century novel follows two sisters who inherit a country estate, and the family's gardener speaks fewer lines than any other recurring character. Each sister in turn persuades him to carry messages, move boundary stones, or repeat stories to the neighbors that serve her side of their quarrel, and each errand is soon undone by the next he runs for the other. The narrator describes him as content to oblige whoever is paying his wages that week. In an often-cited essay, one critic calls the gardener the novel's ______.
worlds.explanation: Both sisters move the gardener about for their own ends, and he obliges whoever pays him, so he is the novel's "pawn." "Prism" fails because the story is not told through his view. "Pivot" fails because each errand is undone by the next, so nothing he does turns the plot. "Puzzle" fails because the narrator explains his behavior.

prism.quote: Each sister in turn persuades him
prism.why: the sisters act on him; the passage gives no sign that events are seen through his eyes

pivot.quote: each errand is soon undone by the next
pivot.why: his acts cancel one another out, so none turns the story

puzzle.quote: content to oblige whoever is paying his wages
puzzle.why: the narrator states his motive, so there is nothing unexplained about him

worlds.passage: A nineteenth-century novel follows two sisters who inherit a country estate, and the family's gardener speaks fewer lines than any other recurring character. In the second chapter he plants a bed of white roses beneath the elder sister's window, the following spring tears every one of them out, and in the last chapter quietly replants them. The narrator, who explains every other character's motives at length, offers no motive for any of these acts, and neither sister ever remarks on the roses. In an often-cited essay, one critic calls the gardener the novel's ______.
worlds.explanation: The gardener plants, uproots and replants the same roses, and the narrator, who explains everyone else, never explains him, so he is the novel's "puzzle." "Prism" fails because the story is not told from his point of view. "Pivot" fails because his acts go unnoticed and change nothing in the plot. "Pawn" fails because no one directs him; he acts on his own, for reasons no one gives.

prism.quote: explains every other character's motives at length
prism.why: the narrator, not the gardener, is the one through whom the characters are presented

pivot.quote: neither sister ever remarks on the roses
pivot.why: his acts pass unnoticed by the main characters, so none changes the course of the plot

pawn.why: he acts alone and unprompted, not at anyone's direction
